extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century religious biography and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close literary-historical evaluation of Muhammad (Mahomet) and the Koran, treating authorial character, textual qualities, doctrinal content, and historical plausibility. The piece judges authenticity, moral force, and literary merit of the prophet and his scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity, in all senses, seems to me the merit of the Koran; it is the first and last merit in a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats sincerity as the primary test of a prophet or scripture: a work that comes from an earnest, genuine heart will reach others and generate other merits. This is used to argue against theories of premeditated imposture or conscious forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary composition and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Koran reads as a wearisome, confused jumble—crude, incondite, with endless iterations and lack of discoverable order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural qualities: organization, chronology, coherence, editing. The text's current order (longest chapters first; fragments on shoulder-blades, etc.) makes it toilsome for European readers; reading in historical sequence might improve comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity / heart-felt voice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book come from the heart, it will contrive to reach other hearts; all art and author-craft are of small amount to that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize whether the writing carries a genuine, felt conviction over polished rhetorical technique. Emotional/direct conviction can compensate for poor formal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic earnestness and depth of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero (prophet) is distinguished by looking through the shows of things into things; being in earnest and unable to live in mere hearsay or formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the figure exhibits an inward seriousness, capacity for original insight, and a compulsive need to express fundamental truths rather than repeat received formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral doctrine: resignation/submission to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Islam's core is submission to God (resignation, denial/annihilation of self); to accept God's will as the wisest and best is the highest wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge doctrinal merit by its capacity to orient moral life toward co-operation with the perceived law of the world; this moral posture is presented as a profound ethical test of a religion's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity from life-history and lack of opportunistic ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The late onset of public mission (fortieth year) and prior peaceful, honest life argue against imposture and for genuine vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biographical facts—timing of claims, prior character, and life pattern—to assess whether a leader's claims are plausibly sincere rather than opportunistic ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of propagation are not conclusive of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a religion spreads by the sword or by persuasion does not determine its truth; every new opinion starts as a minority and will propagate as it can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating violent expansion with falsehood or peaceful spread with truth; historical contingencies (power available to a movement) shape propagation modes and are not definitive evidence of veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and fruitfulness of truth (Nature as umpire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is the ultimate judge: if something is genuine (has wheat), it will grow and persist, even if mixed with chaff; the essence of truth never dies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims and doctrines by their long-term vitality and ability to produce living results in human societies rather than by their initial purity or the amount of 'chaff' mixed in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character: trustworthiness and fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal virtues (named 'Al Amin'—the Faithful) —truth, fidelity, reliability—are central to judging a leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess observable conduct (truthfulness in dealings, loyalty, reputation) as evidence for or against the genuineness of a religious teacher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles not necessary evidence of prophetic authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mahomet often answered 'I can work no miracles.' The absence of miracles does not invalidate prophetic claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require supernatural signs as the sole or decisive test of a prophet; ordinary perception of the world and moral insight may be the relevant standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual transmission and editorial arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Koran was compiled from scattered fragments, often without chronological order; earliest portions were shortest and now lie near the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the effects of compilation, ordering, and transmission on perceived coherence and literary quality; better understanding may come from reconstructing historical sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and traditional narrative use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Koran repeatedly returns to old stories of the Prophets, often iterating the same materials many times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the rhetorical and pastoral role of repetition: it can be consoling and central to appeal, though it may appear wearisome or unskilled to some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary poetic insight and vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Amidst the incondite masses there are stray glances of true insight and poetic images (clouds, cattle, ships) revealing direct perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value isolated passages of striking imagery or insight as signs of a living mind even where overall composition is rough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of formal education as an authenticity marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Mahomet had no school-learning and probably could not write; his teaching stems from life and direct experience rather than learned artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat absence of formal scholarship as potential evidence of originality and authenticity (ideas arising from lived experience), while also acknowledging its effects on style and composition.
